docs.title: Fréchet
docs.text:
Fréchet is a tiny, dependency-free Python package for computing Fréchet bounds — the tightest possible lower and upper bounds on the probability of an intersection, union, or conditional event when all you know are the marginal probabilities.

That constraint is the whole point. The usual tools of probability require a joint distribution. Fréchet bounds require almost nothing, which makes them a good fit for zero-data analytics: auditing numbers, sanity-checking a model, or reasoning about a system whose raw data you cannot see.

How is "Fréchet" pronounced?

Click on the 🔊 icon to listen.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Fréchet has no runtime dependencies and supports Python 3.7 and newer.

From sourceDirectly from GitHub 
git clone https://github.com/galenseilis/frechet.git
cd frechet
pip install -e .

pip install "git+https://github.com/galenseilis/frechet.git"

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
Every public function returns a (lower, upper) tuple of Fréchet bounds.

>>> from frechet.main import intersection, union
>>> intersection([0.5, 0.95])
(0.44999999999999996, 0.5)
>>> union([0.1, 0.05, 0.03333333333333333])
(0.1, 0.18333333333333335)

The intersection of two events is between 0.45 and 0.5; their union is between 0.1 and 0.18. Those are the sharpest statements you can make from the marginals alone.

docs.title: Mathematical background
docs.text: This page explains why the package works the way it does. Read it if you want to understand the mathematics, the notation, and the design decisions — not if you just need to call a function (the how-to guides are better for that).

docs.title: The problem: reasoning from marginals alone
docs.text:
Suppose you know the probability of each event in a family A_1, …, A_n but you do not know how the events relate to one another. The events might overlap heavily, be nearly disjoint, or anything in between. The Fréchet inequalities give the tightest bounds on the probability of their intersection and union that hold for every possible joint distribution consistent with those marginals.

This is what makes the package useful for zero-data analytics: when a summary statistic is available but the raw data is not, you can still make a defensible statement rather than guessing.

docs.title: The two inequalities
docs.text:
There are two such inequalities. One bounds the intersection of events, and the other bounds the union.

\[ \begin{align} \max \left( 0, \sum_{k=1}^n \Pr[A_k] - (n-1) \right) \;\le\; & \Pr \left[ \bigcap_{k=1}^n A_k \right] \;\le\; \min_k \left\{ \Pr[A_k] \right\}, \\ \max \left\{ \Pr[A_k] \right\} \;\le\; & \Pr \left[ \bigcup_{k=1}^n A_k \right] \;\le\; \min \left( 1, \sum_{k=1}^n \Pr[A_k] \right). \end{align} \]

The lower intersection bound is the inclusion–exclusion principle pushed to its limit: if the marginals sum to more than 1, the excess must lie in the overlap. The upper union bound is the complementary fact: the union can never exceed one, nor the sum of the parts.

Here is a public domain portrait of Maurice Fréchet.

docs.title: A note on notation
docs.text: You may notice that these docs use the set-theoretic symbols ∩ and ∪ rather than the logical connectives ∧ and ∨. In many settings they can be used interchangeably, but formal probability theory is defined on sets, so we prefer the set-theoretic notation.

docs.title: The independence gap
docs.text:
What it measures

The independence gap quantifies statistical dependence. The Fréchet inequalities put lower and upper bounds on how much dependence there could be, given only the marginal probabilities.

The independence gap was conceived of sometime between asking A formal definition of a "measure of association" and posting this answer to that question. It was originally defined in terms of cumulative distribution functions, but Sextus Empiricus readily generalised it to events from any probability space in their answer to Is the pairwise independence gap bounded to \([-1/4, 1/4]\)? What about for n variables?.

For events E_1, …, E_n from a suitable probability space (Ω, 𝓕, P), the independence gap is

\[ \phi[E_1, \ldots, E_n] \triangleq \Pr\left[ \bigcap_{k=1}^n E_k \right] - \prod_{k=1}^n \Pr[E_k]. \]

Statistical independence of the collection is exactly the equality

\[ \Pr\left[ \bigcap_{k=1}^n E_k \right] = \prod_{k=1}^n \Pr[E_k], \]

so the gap measures independence directly from its definition:

  • a value of zero means the events are statistically independent,
  • a positive value means the joint probability is larger than independence would predict,
  • a negative value means the joint probability is smaller.

Because the Fréchet bounds on the intersection always contain the product ∏ Pr[E_k], the resulting bounds on the gap always cover zero. That is why you cannot use it to rule out independence.

Ruling out independence is impossible

One might naïvely hope that the bounds could rule out statistical independence, but they cannot. The bounds will always cover zero.

docs.title: The almost-disjoint gap
docs.text:
What it measures

The almost-disjoint gap quantifies how close a collection of events is to being disjoint (mutually exclusive). The Fréchet inequalities provide bounds that can be normalised into a score.

In Can we obtain a probability interpretation on these bounds obtained from the ADG and Frechet inequalities?, the almost-disjoint gap (ADG) is defined as

Quote

The almost-disjoint gap is given by

\[ \mathcal{D}_{\mu} \left( E_1, \ldots, E_n \right) \triangleq \mu \left( \bigcup_{k=1}^{n} E_k \right) - \sum_{k=1}^n \mu \left( E_k \right), \]

where μ is a measure and {E_k} are elements of a suitable σ-algebra. When the ADG equals zero, the events are almost everywhere pairwise disjoint.

The inclusion–exclusion principle states that

\[ P\left( \bigcup_{k=1}^n E_k \right) = \underbrace{\sum_{k=1}^n P(E_k)}_{\text{marginal terms}} + \underbrace{\sum_{k=2}^n \left((-1)^{k-1} \sum_{\substack{I \subseteq \{1, \ldots, n \} \\ |I| = k}} P\left(\bigcap_{i \in I} E_i \right) \right)}_{\text{joint terms}}. \]

This shows directly what the ADG means: it is exactly the sum of the joint terms.

\[ \mathcal{D}_{P} \left( E_1, \ldots, E_n \right) = \underbrace{\sum_{k=2}^n \left((-1)^{k-1} \sum_{\substack{I \subseteq \{1, \ldots, n \} \\ |I| = k}} P\left(\bigcap_{i \in I} E_i \right) \right)}_{\text{joint terms}}. \]

Combining the ADG with the Fréchet union inequality bounds the ADG in terms of the marginals:

\[ \max \{ P(E_k) \} - \sum_{k=1}^n P ( E_k ) \;\le\; \mathcal{D}_{P} \left( E_1, \ldots, E_n \right) \;\le\; \min \left(1, \sum_{k=1}^n P(E_k) \right) - \sum_{k=1}^n P ( E_k ). \]

Not knowing the marginals, the most extreme bounds depend only on the number of events:

\[ 1 - n \;\le\; \mathcal{D}_{P} \left( E_1, \ldots, E_n \right) \;\le\; 0. \]

docs.title: Normalising the almost-disjoint gap
docs.text:
Since 1 - n ≤ 0, we can flip the bounds by multiplying by -1:

\[ 0 \;\le\; -\mathcal{D}_{P} \left( E_1, \ldots, E_n \right) \;\le\; n-1. \]

Because n - 1 can exceed one, divide through by n - 1 to normalise onto the unit interval:

\[ 0 \;\le\; \frac{-\mathcal{D}_{P} \left( E_1, \ldots, E_n \right)}{n-1} \;\le\; 1. \]

docs.title: Where this is useful
docs.text: The primary applications are in data analysis where the appropriate summary statistics are available but the raw data is not. Typical situations include auditing reported figures, sanity-checking a model against partial information, or reasoning about a system you cannot access directly.

docs.title: Design philosophy
docs.text:
Fréchet is designed to work with minimal dependencies. Because the primary use case is to work with summary statistics, dealing with truly "big data" is out of scope. The package therefore uses no special packages or language extensions — only the Python standard library.

Is Fréchet compatible with PyPy?

Fréchet appears to work with PyPy, but this is not a supported compatibility guarantee.

docs.title: Worked examples
docs.text:
These examples show the Fréchet bounds applied end to end. They are understanding-oriented: the point is to build intuition for what the bounds mean, not to teach the API. Every number below is produced by the package.

Warning

The numbers on this page are made up and should not be used for any real-world decision.

docs.title: The Linda problem
docs.text:
A conjunction fallacy is an inference that the intersection of two or more events is more probable than any event alone. Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman raised awareness of this in the form of the Linda problem:

Quote

Linda is 31 years old, single, outspoken, and very bright. She majored in philosophy. As a student, she was deeply concerned with issues of discrimination and social justice, and also participated in anti-nuclear demonstrations.

Which is more probable?

  1. Linda is a bank teller.
  2. Linda is a bank teller and is active in the feminist movement.

A non-trivial fraction of participants pick option 2, even though it is logically impossible: an intersection is a subset of each of its parts, so

\[ \Pr[A \cap B] \le \min\bigl(\Pr[A],\, \Pr[B]\bigr). \]

Suppose Pr[A] = 1/2 and Pr[B] = 19/20. The upper bound is

\[ \Pr[A \cap B] \le \min\left(\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{19}{20}\right) = \tfrac{1}{2}. \]

The lower bound comes from the inclusion–exclusion squeeze:

\[ \max\left(0,\ \Pr[A] + \Pr[B] - 1\right) = \tfrac{9}{20}. \]

So Pr[A ∩ B] ∈ [9/20, 1/2]. The package agrees:

>>> from frechet.main import intersection
>>> intersection([1/2, 19/20])
(0.44999999999999996, 0.5)

docs.title: Bad weather at the picnic
docs.text:
You are planning a picnic and define "bad weather" as precipitation (PPT), high winds (HW), or temperatures outside [20, 30] °C (ET). You only have marginals:

\[ \Pr[\text{PPT}] = \tfrac{1}{10}, \quad \Pr[\text{HW}] = \tfrac{1}{20}, \quad \Pr[\text{ET}] = \tfrac{1}{30}. \]

The Fréchet union bounds give

\[ \max\left\{ \Pr[\text{PPT}], \Pr[\text{HW}], \Pr[\text{ET}] \right\} = \tfrac{1}{10} \;\le\; \Pr[\text{PPT} \cup \text{HW} \cup \text{ET}], \] \[ \Pr[\text{PPT} \cup \text{HW} \cup \text{ET}] \;\le\; \min\left(1, \tfrac{1}{10} + \tfrac{1}{20} + \tfrac{1}{30}\right) = \tfrac{11}{60}. \]

So the chance of bad weather is somewhere in [1/10, 11/60], roughly 10% to 18%:

>>> from frechet.main import union
>>> union([1/10, 1/20, 1/30])
(0.1, 0.18333333333333335)

docs.title: Diagnostic screening
docs.text:
A screening test is meant to detect a condition D from a symptom S. You know that 40% of a population has the condition and 70% has the symptom, but the joint occurrence Pr[D ∩ S] is not recorded. What can you say about Pr[D | S]?

First bound the numerator, the joint probability:

>>> from frechet.main import intersection
>>> intersection([0.4, 0.7])
(0.10000000000000009, 0.4)

At least 10% of people must have both, and at most 40%. Now divide by Pr[S] = 0.7:

>>> from frechet.main import conditional
>>> conditional([0.4, 0.7], [0.7])
(0.142857142857143, 0.5714285714285715)

So Pr[D | S] lies between about 14% and 57%. The interval is wide, and that width is the honest answer: without the joint distribution, no sharper claim is possible.

This is also a caution. If the symptom is common and the condition is not strongly associated with it, the conditional probability can be far from the 100% that a "positive screen" might suggest.

Why the lower bound is not zero here

The lower bound is positive only because the marginals sum to more than one (0.4 + 0.7 = 1.1). When they do not, the overlap could be empty and the lower bound collapses to zero.

docs.title: Compute bounds on a conditional probability
docs.text: This guide shows you how to bound Pr[numerator | denominator] from marginal probabilities, choosing the set operator used on each side.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: You need bounds on a conditional probability such as Pr[A ∩ B | C ∪ D], but you only have the marginal probabilities of A, B, C, and D.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Call conditional with the numerator probabilities, the denominator probabilities, and the operator to apply on each side. Operators are named 'intersection' (the default) or 'union'.

>>> from frechet.main import conditional
>>> conditional([0.2, 0.3], [0.5], lop='union', rop='intersection')
(0.6, 1.0)

The bounds are computed by bounding the numerator and the denominator separately and then dividing:

\[ \frac{\text{numerator}_{\text{lower}}}{\text{denominator}_{\text{upper}}} \;\le\; \Pr[\text{numerator} \mid \text{denominator}] \;\le\; \frac{\text{numerator}_{\text{upper}}}{\text{denominator}_{\text{lower}}}. \]

docs.title: Choosing operators
docs.text:
Desired quantity Call Pr[A ∩ B | C ∩ D] conditional([a, b], [c, d]) Pr[A ∪ B | C ∩ D] conditional([a, b], [c, d], lop='union') Pr[A ∩ B | C ∪ D] conditional([a, b], [c, d], rop='union') Pr[A ∪ B | C ∪ D] conditional([a, b], [c, d], lop='union', rop='union')

Passing any other operator name raises NotImplementedError:

>>> conditional([0.5], [0.5], lop='xor')
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
NotImplementedError: Operator xor not implemented.

docs.title: A zero lower denominator bound raises
docs.text:
The upper bound divides by the denominator's lower bound. When that bound is 0, Python raises ZeroDivisionError.

>>> conditional([0.1], [0.1, 0.2])
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
ZeroDivisionError: float division by zero

The denominator here is Pr[C ∩ D], whose lower bound is 0, so no finite upper bound on the ratio can be derived this way. Guard against it by checking intersection(...) before calling, or by choosing rop='union' when the denominator is a union.

docs.title: The interval may extend past [0, 1]
docs.text:
Because the package divides interval endpoints independently, the resulting interval is a conservative over-approximation and can spill outside [0, 1]:

>>> conditional([0.6], [0.8, 0.7])
(0.8571428571428572, 1.2)

A probability cannot exceed 1, so you may clamp the bounds yourself if your application requires it. The over-approximation is intentional: it stays valid without assuming dependence between the numerator and denominator.

docs.title: Measure independence and disjointness
docs.text: This guide shows you how to quantify statistical dependence and how close a collection of events is to being mutually exclusive, using only marginal probabilities.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: You want a single number describing whether events are independent (Pr[A ∩ B] = Pr[A] · Pr[B]) or almost disjoint (Pr[A ∪ B] = Pr[A] + Pr[B]), but you only have the marginals.

docs.title: Solution: independence gap
docs.text:
The independence gap is Pr[A ∩ B] - Pr[A] · Pr[B]. Bounding the intersection and subtracting the product gives bounds on the gap.

>>> from frechet.main import independence_gap
>>> independence_gap([0.5, 0.2])
(-0.1, 0.1)
>>> independence_gap([0.5, 0.5])
(-0.25, 0.25)

Interpretation:

  • 0 inside the interval is unavoidable — marginals can never rule out independence, because the interval always contains 0.
  • A positive value means the joint probability is larger than independence would predict (positively associated).
  • A negative value means it is smaller (negatively associated).
  • For two events the gap always lies within [-1/4, 1/4]; the package returns the tighter bounds implied by the marginals you supply.

docs.title: Solution: almost-disjoint gap
docs.text:
The almost-disjoint gap is Pr[A ∪ B] - (Pr[A] + Pr[B]). It is 0 exactly when the events are disjoint, and negative when they overlap.

>>> from frechet.main import almost_disjoint_gap
>>> almost_disjoint_gap([0.2, 0.3])
(-0.2, 0.0)
>>> almost_disjoint_gap([0.1, 0.05, 0.03333333333333333])
(-0.08333333333333334, 0.0)

The upper bound is always 0 (the union can never exceed the sum of the marginals), so a value near 0 means the events are nearly disjoint.

docs.title: Normalise to the unit interval
docs.text:
The theoretical ranges are known, so you can rescale the raw gaps. For the almost-disjoint gap of n events, -(Pr[union] - sum) lies in [0, n - 1]:

>>> from frechet.main import almost_disjoint_gap
>>> lower, upper = almost_disjoint_gap([0.2, 0.3])
>>> n = 2
>>> (-upper / (n - 1), -lower / (n - 1))
(-0.0, 0.2)

A similar normalisation applies to the independence gap; see the mathematical background for the derivation.

docs.title: Watch out
docs.text:
• The gaps are signed. Negative values are meaningful, not errors.
  • The independence gap always covers zero. Do not treat a lower bound greater than zero as evidence of dependence; it cannot occur from marginals.
  • The almost-disjoint gap never has a positive upper bound. If you see one for n ≥ 2, check your inputs.

docs.title: Compute bounds on intersections and unions
docs.text: This guide shows you how to bound the probability that a collection of events all occur (an intersection) or that at least one occurs (a union), given only the marginal probabilities.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: You have marginal probabilities Pr[A_1], …, Pr[A_n] but not the joint distribution, and you need the sharpest possible bounds on Pr[A_1 ∩ … ∩ A_n] or Pr[A_1 ∪ … ∪ A_n].

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Import intersection and union from frechet.main and pass any iterable of probabilities. Each returns a (lower, upper) tuple.

>>> from frechet.main import intersection, union
>>> intersection([0.5, 0.95])
(0.44999999999999996, 0.5)
>>> union([0.5, 0.95])
(0.95, 1.0)

The bounds are:

\[ \max\Bigl(0,\ \sum_k \Pr[A_k] - (n - 1)\Bigr) \;\le\; \Pr\Bigl[\bigcap_k A_k\Bigr] \;\le\; \min_k \bigl\{\Pr[A_k]\bigr\}, \] \[ \max_k \bigl\{\Pr[A_k]\bigr\} \;\le\; \Pr\Bigl[\bigcup_k A_k\Bigr] \;\le\; \min\Bigl(1,\ \sum_k \Pr[A_k]\Bigr). \]

docs.title: More than two events
docs.text:
There is no limit on the number of events; the formulas generalise directly.

>>> intersection([0.7, 0.8, 0.9])
(0.3999999999999999, 0.7)
>>> union([0.1, 0.05, 0.03333333333333333])
(0.1, 0.18333333333333335)

docs.title: Pass a generator or a tuple
docs.text:
The functions accept any Iterable, not just a list. Generators are consumed safely because the input is converted to a list internally.

>>> intersection(x / 10 for x in range(1, 6))
(0.0, 0.1)
>>> union((0.2, 0.3))
(0.3, 0.5)

docs.title: Bound the complement
docs.text:
To bound Pr[¬A ∩ ¬B] (neither event happens), apply the identity Pr[¬A] = 1 - Pr[A] first, then take the intersection.

>>> complement = [1 - p for p in [0.5, 0.95]]
>>> complement
[0.5, 0.050000000000000044]
>>> intersection(complement)
(0.0, 0.05)

docs.title: Watch out
docs.text:
• Empty input raises ValueError. intersection([]) and union([]) need at least one event because they call min/max on the probabilities.
  • Bounds are clamped to [0, 1]. The lower intersection bound is never negative and the upper union bound never exceeds one.
  • Floating-point noise is expected. Results such as 0.44999999999999996 are the closest double-precision value to 0.45. Compare with a tolerance rather than == when writing tests.
  • The bounds can be wide. That width is information: it is the price of knowing only the marginals. For two events the interval collapses only when one event is impossible or certain.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
All public functions live in the frechet.main module. The package root (frechet/__init__.py) is intentionally empty, so always import from the module:

from frechet.main import intersection, union, conditional

Every function accepts any Iterable of marginal probabilities — lists, tuples, and generators all work, because the input is converted to a list internally. Every function returns a (lower, upper) tuple of floats.

docs.text: Function Returns bounds on intersection Pr[A_1 ∩ … ∩ A_n] union Pr[A_1 ∪ … ∪ A_n] conditional Pr[numerator \| denominator] jaccard_index Pr[A ∩ B] / Pr[A ∪ B] independence_gap Pr[A ∩ B] - Pr[A] · Pr[B] almost_disjoint_gap Pr[A ∪ B] - (Pr[A] + Pr[B])

docs.title: Module frechet.main
docs.text:
Fréchet bounds on intersections, unions, and conditional probabilities.

Every public function accepts any iterable of marginal probabilities and returns a (lower, upper) tuple of Fréchet bounds. The package has no runtime dependencies.

The bounds are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9chet_inequalities.

docs.title: intersection
docs.text:
Compute Fréchet bounds for the probability of an intersection of events.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default probs Iterable[float]

Probabilities of the individual events.

required

Returns:

Type Description float

The lower and upper bounds on Pr[A_1 ∩ ... ∩ A_n] as a

float

(lower, upper) tuple.

Source code in src/frechet/main.py 
def intersection(probs: Iterable[float]) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    '''Compute Fréchet bounds for the probability of an intersection of events.

    Args:
        probs: Probabilities of the individual events.

    Returns:
        The lower and upper bounds on ``Pr[A_1 ∩ ... ∩ A_n]`` as a
        ``(lower, upper)`` tuple.
    '''
    probs = list(probs)
    lower = max(0.0, sum(probs) - (len(probs) - 1))
    upper = min(probs)
    return lower, upper

def union(probs: Iterable[float]) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    '''Compute Fréchet bounds for the probability of a union of events.

    Args:
        probs: Probabilities of the individual events.

    Returns:
        The lower and upper bounds on ``Pr[A_1 ∪ ... ∪ A_n]`` as a
        ``(lower, upper)`` tuple.
    '''
    probs = list(probs)
    lower = max(probs)
    upper = min(1.0, sum(probs))
    return lower, upper

docs.title: conditional
docs.text:
Compute Fréchet bounds for a conditional probability.

The conditional probability is bounded by taking the ratio of the bounds on the numerator and the denominator, i.e. left / right.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default lprobs Iterable[float]

Probabilities of the events in the numerator.

required rprobs Iterable[float]

Probabilities of the events in the denominator.

required lop str

Operator applied to lprobs; either 'intersection' or 'union'.

'intersection' rop str

Operator applied to rprobs; either 'intersection' or 'union'.

'intersection'

Returns:

Type Description float

The lower and upper bounds on the conditional probability as a

float

(lower, upper) tuple.

Raises:

Type Description NotImplementedError

If lop or rop is not a supported operator.

Source code in src/frechet/main.py 
def conditional(
    lprobs: Iterable[float],
    rprobs: Iterable[float],
    lop: str = 'intersection',
    rop: str = 'intersection',
) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    '''Compute Fréchet bounds for a conditional probability.

    The conditional probability is bounded by taking the ratio of the bounds
    on the numerator and the denominator, i.e. ``left / right``.

    Args:
        lprobs: Probabilities of the events in the numerator.
        rprobs: Probabilities of the events in the denominator.
        lop: Operator applied to ``lprobs``; either ``'intersection'`` or
            ``'union'``.
        rop: Operator applied to ``rprobs``; either ``'intersection'`` or
            ``'union'``.

    Returns:
        The lower and upper bounds on the conditional probability as a
        ``(lower, upper)`` tuple.

    Raises:
        NotImplementedError: If ``lop`` or ``rop`` is not a supported operator.
    '''
    if lop == 'intersection':
        left_lower, left_upper = intersection(lprobs)
    elif lop == 'union':
        left_lower, left_upper = union(lprobs)
    else:
        raise NotImplementedError(f'Operator {lop} not implemented.')

    if rop == 'intersection':
        right_lower, right_upper = intersection(rprobs)
    elif rop == 'union':
        right_lower, right_upper = union(rprobs)
    else:
        raise NotImplementedError(f'Operator {rop} not implemented.')

    lower = left_lower / right_upper
    upper = left_upper / right_lower
    return lower, upper

docs.title: jaccard_index
docs.text:
Compute Fréchet bounds for the Jaccard index.

The Jaccard index is the ratio of the intersection to the union, so its bounds are obtained by dividing the intersection bounds by the union bounds.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default probs Iterable[float]

Probabilities of the individual events.

required

Returns:

Type Description float

The lower and upper bounds on the Jaccard index as a (lower, upper)

float

tuple.

Source code in src/frechet/main.py 
def jaccard_index(probs: Iterable[float]) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    '''Compute Fréchet bounds for the Jaccard index.

    The Jaccard index is the ratio of the intersection to the union, so its
    bounds are obtained by dividing the intersection bounds by the union
    bounds.

    Args:
        probs: Probabilities of the individual events.

    Returns:
        The lower and upper bounds on the Jaccard index as a ``(lower, upper)``
        tuple.
    '''
    probs = list(probs)
    intersection_lower, intersection_upper = intersection(probs)
    union_lower, union_upper = union(probs)
    return intersection_lower / union_upper, intersection_upper / union_lower

docs.title: independence_gap
docs.text:
Compute Fréchet bounds for the independence gap.

The independence gap is the joint probability of the events minus the product of their marginal probabilities. Its bounds are obtained by subtracting the product of the marginal probabilities from the bounds on the intersection.

(lower, upper) tuple.

def independence_gap(probs: Iterable[float]) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    '''Compute Fréchet bounds for the independence gap.

    The independence gap is the joint probability of the events minus the
    product of their marginal probabilities. Its bounds are obtained by
    subtracting the product of the marginal probabilities from the bounds on
    the intersection.

    Args:
        probs: Probabilities of the individual events.

    Returns:
        The lower and upper bounds on the independence gap as a
        ``(lower, upper)`` tuple.
    '''
    probs = list(probs)
    intersection_lower, intersection_upper = intersection(probs)
    product = 1.0
    for prob in probs:
        product *= prob
    return intersection_lower - product, intersection_upper - product

def almost_disjoint_gap(probs: Iterable[float]) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    '''Compute Fréchet bounds for the almost-disjoint gap.

    The almost-disjoint gap is the probability of the union of the events
    minus the sum of their marginal probabilities. Its bounds are obtained by
    subtracting the sum of the marginal probabilities from the bounds on the
    union.

    Args:
        probs: Probabilities of the individual events.

    Returns:
        The lower and upper bounds on the almost-disjoint gap as a
        ``(lower, upper)`` tuple.
    '''
    probs = list(probs)
    union_lower, union_upper = union(probs)
    total = sum(probs)
    return union_lower - total, union_upper - total

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
This tutorial walks you through the Fréchet package from an empty Python session to every function it offers. You will compute bounds by hand first, then verify the package agrees.

No probability background is assumed beyond the idea that probabilities are numbers between 0 and 1.

docs.title: What you will build
docs.text:
By the end of this tutorial you will have computed, for the same collection of events:

  • the bounds on the probability that all of them happen (an intersection),
  • the bounds on the probability that at least one happens (a union),
  • the bounds on a conditional probability,
  • scores that describe how dependent and how almost disjoint the events are.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Install the package from a checkout of the repository:

git clone https://github.com/galenseilis/frechet.git
cd frechet
pip install -e .

You can confirm it worked by importing the library. In a fresh Python session:

>>> from frechet.main import intersection

If that line runs without error, you are ready.

docs.title: Step 1: Bounds on an intersection
docs.text:
Imagine a weather service tells you two marginal probabilities for next Saturday: a 50% chance of rain and a 95% chance of wind. It does not tell you the chance of rain and wind. What can you say anyway?

Write down what you know. Let A be "it rains" and B be "it is windy", with Pr[A] = 0.5 and Pr[B] = 0.95. The Fréchet inequalities say the joint probability Pr[A ∩ B] is squeezed between two values:

\[ \max\bigl(0,\ \Pr[A] + \Pr[B] - 1\bigr) \;\le\; \Pr[A \cap B] \;\le\; \min\bigl(\Pr[A], \Pr[B]\bigr). \]

By hand, the lower bound is 0.5 + 0.95 - 1 = 0.45, and the upper bound is min(0.5, 0.95) = 0.5. Now let the package do it:

>>> from frechet.main import intersection
>>> intersection([0.5, 0.95])
(0.44999999999999996, 0.5)

The first number is the lower bound, the second is the upper bound. So there is between a 45% and a 50% chance of rain and wind. The lone floating-point digit is just how 0.45 is stored internally; treat the result as (0.45, 0.5).

The same idea works for any number of events:

>>> intersection([0.7, 0.8, 0.9])
(0.3999999999999999, 0.7)

docs.title: Step 2: Bounds on a union
docs.text:
Now ask the other question: what is the chance of rain or wind or both? The bounds are

\[ \max_k \bigl\{\Pr[A_k]\bigr\} \;\le\; \Pr\Bigl[\bigcup_k A_k\Bigr] \;\le\; \min\Bigl(1,\ \sum_k \Pr[A_k]\Bigr). \] 
>>> from frechet.main import union
>>> union([0.5, 0.95])
(0.95, 1.0)

The union is almost certain, somewhere between 95% and 100%. Notice the upper bound was capped at 1. Add a third event and the cap still applies:

>>> union([0.6, 0.7])
(0.7, 1.0)

docs.title: Step 3: Conditional probability bounds
docs.text:
Conditional probability is a ratio, Pr[A | B] = Pr[A ∩ B] / Pr[B]. To bound it, the package bounds the numerator and denominator and divides.

By default both sides are treated as intersections:

>>> from frechet.main import conditional
>>> conditional([0.4], [0.8])
(0.5, 0.5)

Here Pr[A | B] is exactly 0.5 because both pieces were single events.

Real problems mix operators. Suppose you want Pr[A ∩ B | C ∪ D]. Pass the operator names 'intersection' or 'union' for each side:

>>> conditional([0.2, 0.3], [0.5], lop='union', rop='intersection')
(0.6, 1.0)

The numerator is a union (0.2 ∪ 0.3), and the denominator is the single event 0.5. You will learn more about the operator arguments in the conditional probability how-to.

docs.title: Step 4: Measuring dependence
docs.text:
Two events are independent when Pr[A ∩ B] = Pr[A] · Pr[B]. The independence gap is the difference between the joint probability and that product, and the package bounds it for you:

>>> from frechet.main import independence_gap
>>> independence_gap([0.5, 0.5])
(-0.25, 0.25)

The bounds always straddle zero, so marginals alone can never prove that events depend on one another. They only tell you how far dependence could go.

docs.title: Step 5: Measuring near-disjointness
docs.text:
Finally, the almost-disjoint gap measures how far a collection is from being mutually exclusive. It is the union minus the sum of the marginals:

>>> from frechet.main import almost_disjoint_gap
>>> almost_disjoint_gap([0.2, 0.3])
(-0.2, 0.0)

A value of 0 would mean the events never overlap. Read more about both scores in the independence and disjointness how-to.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
You have now used every function in the package. From here:

  • Solve a concrete task with the how-to guides.
  • Look up exact signatures in the API reference.
  • Learn why the formulas look the way they do in the mathematical background.
